title: We need to talk about the lawyers who threaten free speech in Britain
gist: Bellingcat founder Eliot Higgins argues the Solicitors Regulation Authority has failed to hold law firms accountable for SLAPPs, and that a September High Court ruling stripping its access to legally privileged material will leave it 'toothless'. He uses his own £70,000 defence against a Prigozhin defamation claim brought by Discreet Law to call for a more proactive, transparent SRA ahead of its Supreme Court appeal.

themes.theme: SRA weakened by High Court ruling

insights.claim: On 21 September the High Court ruled that the Solicitors Regulation Authority no longer has power to access legally privileged materials when investigating complaints, which the UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition says renders it 'toothless'.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Weaker regulatory oversight of solicitors lowers the risk for law firms pursuing aggressive litigation for wealthy clients.

insights.claim: The SRA is preparing to appeal to the Supreme Court to reclaim its power to access privileged materials.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: The Supreme Court outcome is a key catalyst for UK legal-sector regulation and SLAPP accountability.
insights.locator: As the SRA prepares for its appeal

insights.claim: Despite several disciplinary tribunal proceedings, no lawyer or firm has ultimately been found by the SRA to have breached obligations related to SLAPPs.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Enforcement against SLAPP-enabling law firms has so far been nil, signalling low regulatory risk for that practice area.
insights.quote: no individual lawyer or firm has been found by the Solicitors Regulation Authority (SRA) to have ultimately breached their obligations related to SLAPPs

insights.claim: How the SRA proceeds will determine whether freedom of expression is protected in the UK.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: UK investigative journalism and public-interest scrutiny of powerful actors depend on SLAPP enforcement.
insights.locator: How the SRA proceeds from here

insights.claim: In December 2021, sanctioned Russian oligarch Yevgeny Prigozhin sued Eliot Higgins for defamation in a British court over tweets linking him to the Wagner Group, which only repeated what CNN, Der Spiegel and Bellingcat had reported.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: UK courts have been usable by sanctioned foreign actors to pressure critics, a reputational issue for London's legal market.
insights.quote: A British citizen was being sued in a British court, by a sanctioned Russian warlord, for saying what the British government had already said.

insights.claim: British law firm Discreet Law led Prigozhin's case and withdrew in March 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine; the claim was struck out in May 2022.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Shows how sanctions and geopolitical shocks can abruptly end UK representation of Russian clients.
insights.locator: My own experience with the SRA

insights.claim: Higgins's legal fees reached roughly £70,000 with no realistic prospect of recovery from a sanctioned individual, a prospect that ended with Prigozhin's death in August 2023.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: SLAPPs impose unrecoverable costs on defendants even when claims collapse, the core mechanism of their chilling effect.
insights.quote: my legal fees had amounted to roughly £70,000

insights.claim: Prigozhin publicly admitted founding Wagner in September 2022, after his defamation claim against Higgins had collapsed.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Illustrates the bad-faith nature of the claim the SRA declined to act on.

insights.claim: Nearly two years after Higgins's complaint, the SRA took no action, saying there was no evidence Discreet Law knew or should have known its instructions were false; this explanation came only via a letter to Baroness Stowell.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Slow, opaque regulatory outcomes reduce deterrence against abusive litigation.
insights.quote: there was no evidence to suggest the firm were aware, or should have been aware, that the instructions they received were false
insights.locator: But in this case, nearly two years

insights.claim: The SRA's 2024/25 annual report says it has received about 300 reports of abusive litigation since 2022, opened formal investigations in 97 and has 31 still open, but does not say how many involved SLAPPs.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Inconsistent regulatory data makes the scale of SLAPP activity in the UK hard to measure.
insights.quote: we have received approximately 300 reports about abusive litigation, some raising allegations of SLAPPs, and have proceeded to formal investigation in 97 cases. Of these, 31 remain open.
insights.locator: As noted by the UK Anti-SLAPP

insights.claim: A regulator cannot be trusted if it operates inside a black box, and the SRA does not publish SLAPP complaint data regularly or consistently.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Transparency reforms at the SRA would be a signal of tougher oversight of the legal sector.
insights.quote: For a regulatory body to be trusted, it cannot operate inside a black box.

insights.claim: The UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition has seen solicitors' letters threatening critics with police investigations, bankruptcy and jail, and one firm invoking intellectual property rights to stop a campaigner sharing its letter, yet the SRA did not progress these complaints.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Intimidatory legal tactics continue largely unchecked, sustaining reputational risk for firms involved.
insights.locator: The UK Anti-SLAPP Coalition also has concerns

insights.claim: Several SLAPP targets report waiting years for SRA outcomes, and many have simply given up.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Slow redress means SLAPPs succeed in silencing targets regardless of eventual outcomes.
insights.locator: Several SLAPP targets who have spoken

insights.claim: Fighting SLAPPs requires scrutiny of the law firms that bring them, not only legislative change.
insights.speaker: Eliot Higgins
insights.so_what: Points to professional-conduct regulation as the next front in UK anti-SLAPP policy.
insights.locator: In the fight for freedom of speech
